unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 9 of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. This unit is all about secret messages — how we can hide the meaning of a message so that only the right person can read it. The big idea is the cipher: a set of rules for turning a normal message into a secret one, and back again. There are two important new words. Plain text is the normal, easy-to-read message, like hello. Ciphertext is the secret, scrambled version that only makes sense if you know the cipher. A cipher is the rule that turns one into the other, and both friends know the rule; anyone else just sees a jumble. We say we encode a message to make it secret, and decode it to read it again.

outcomes: Explain what a cipher is — a set of rules that turns plain text into ciphertext.
Tell the difference between plain text (the normal message) and ciphertext (the secret message).
Encode a short message using a simple code (make it secret).
Decode a short secret message back into plain text (read it).
Use at least two different codes: the flip-text cipher, a picture code, the letters-to-numbers code, and the reverse-alphabet code.
Say why we might use a cipher when sending information on a network.

concepts.title: What is a cipher? Plain text and ciphertext
concepts.explanation: A cipher is a set of rules that turns a normal message into a secret one. The normal message is called plain text. The secret, scrambled message is called ciphertext. Both friends know the rule, so both can read it — but nobody else can. Have you ever wanted to tell your best friend something so that nobody else understands? Today we learn how to send secret messages — like a real spy or a code-breaker! before the vowel sound in a word, so. It does not have to be perfect — it is just to show that a secret language follows a rule.
concepts.example: Answer this in your own words, out loud or on paper: What is a cipher? Plain text and ciphertext? Then check your answer against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you point to where the cipher (the rule) does its work? Do not expect you to encode anything yet — that starts next session.

concepts.title: The flip-text cipher
concepts.explanation: Our first real cipher is the flip-text cipher. The rule is simple: write the whole message backwards; to read it, flip it back. It is a great first code because there is no chart to remember — the rule *is* the code. write the letters in the opposite order: smeg. Same letters — just backwards. Now it is secret!
concepts.example: Find one real example of the flip-text cipher around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you check your work by flipping back? Neat, careful letter-by-letter work matters more than speed here. Do you keep every letter (none dropped, none added) when you flip?

concepts.title: Picture codes: swapping letters for symbols
concepts.explanation: A code can swap each letter for something else — not just another letter, but a little picture or symbol. We use a key (a chart) that shows what each letter becomes. As long as both friends have the same key, they can read each other's secret pictures. Encode meet together, drawing square, triangle, triangle, diamond. Then ask a child to be the decoder and read the pictures back using the key.
concepts.example: Find one real example of picture codes: swapping letters for symbols around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you keep the shapes in the correct order (left to right), just like letters in a word? Do you use the key carefully, matching each picture to the right letter? Praise neat, in-order drawing.

concepts.title: The letters-to-numbers code
concepts.explanation:
We can swap each letter for a number. The rule is: a = 01, b = 02, c = 03, all the way to z = 26. We always use two digits (so 05, not 5) to keep the message tidy. This is the letters-to-numbers code.

encode a word slowly: cat is c = 03, a = 01, t = 20, so cat becomes 03 01 20. Then decode one together: write 08 09 and you can look up h and i to read hi. Put the big number chart on the wall and count along it together: a is 1, b is 2, c is 3.
concepts.example: Find one real example of the letters-to-numbers code around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you keep a small gap between letters so the numbers do not run together? Careful place-keeping is the whole skill here. Do you use two digits for every letter?

concepts.title: The reverse-alphabet code, and being a code-breaker
concepts.explanation: In this code each letter is matched with the letter from the other end of the alphabet: a = z, b = y, c = x, and so on. It is the letters-to-letters code. The best surprise: the same rule hides *and* reveals, so encoding and decoding are the same action. These two are partners. Then, to show the magic, encode svool again — it turns back into hello.
concepts.example: You can gasp; it feels like real code-breaking. Write the alphabet forwards, then underneath write it backwards, so the pairs line up.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you notice that the same rule decodes and encodes? In Task 8, Can you describe the pattern (front letter pairs with back letter) in your own words? Can you use the paired chart both ways?

esafety.title: Keep personal information private
esafety.text: Your full name, address, school, phone number, birthday and passwords are personal information. Never type them into a game, an app or a website, and never send them to someone you only know online.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

selfAssessment: I can explain what a cipher is — a set of rules that turns plain text into ciphertext.
I can tell the difference between plain text (the normal message) and ciphertext (the secret message).
I can encode a short message using a simple code (make it secret).
I can decode a short secret message back into plain text (read it).
I can use at least two different codes: the flip-text cipher, a picture code, the letters-to-numbers code, and the reverse-alphabet code.
I can say why we might use a cipher when sending information on a network.
